title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
Setting: P is prime, a is an integer with 1 ≤ a < P, and the 'series of residues' is the list 1, α, β, γ, … of distinct least residues of 1, a, a², … mod P. In modern terms this is the cyclic subgroup ⟨a⟩ of (Z/PZ)*. The page uses three facts from the previous page: the residues repeat with period r (the order of a); some power of a leaves remainder 1; and by the coset argument of §22, r divides P−1.

(§23, end) Since 1, a, …, a^{r−1} give the r distinct residues, the next power gives a^r ≡ 1, so P | a^r − 1. Write P−1 = kr. Then a^{P−1} − 1 = (a^r)^k − 1 is divisible by a^r − 1, and hence by P. This is Fermat's little theorem, obtained via Lagrange's theorem applied to the cyclic subgroup.

(§24) If a^m ≡ μ and a^n ≡ ν, then a^{m+n} ≡ μν. So the residue set is closed under multiplication mod P, and therefore under products of any number of factors and under powers. Euler introduces the notation '..P' to mean 'some integer multiple of P'.

(§25) Given residues μ ≡ a^m and ν ≡ a^n, set ω ≡ a^{n−m}, or a^{P−1+n−m} when n < m (this is legitimate by §23). Then ν ≡ μω mod P, so quotients exist within the set.

(§26, beginning, completed on the next page) Since 1 always belongs to the set, every μ has a partner ω with μω ≡ 1, which Euler calls 'socii'. Together §§24–26 show that the residues of powers of a form a subgroup of the multiplicative group mod P. These are preliminaries to §28, where Euler proves that x^n ≡ 1 has at most n solutions mod P, as a step toward his results on power residues and primitive roots.
errors: No error on this page. A small gap in the supporting §22 (previous page): the claim that a non-residue 𝔄 yields r distinct non-residues α𝔄, β𝔄, … tacitly needs cancellation mod a prime (μ𝔄 ≡ ν𝔄 ⇒ μ ≡ ν). Euler does not state this.
In §25, using a^{P−1+n−m} when n<m relies on §23 (a^{P−1} ≡ 1). This is valid; a^{r+n−m} would serve equally well.

ideas.what: Fermat's little theorem deduced from the order r of a dividing P−1, since a^r−1 divides a^{P−1}−1.
ideas.modern_name: Fermat's little theorem via Lagrange's theorem for cyclic subgroups
ideas.usually_credited_to: Fermat (statement, 1640); Euler (group-theoretic proof, Theoremata circa residua, E262, c.1758/1761)

ideas.what: Residues of powers of a are closed under multiplication, quotients, and inverses ('socia').
ideas.modern_name: ⟨a⟩ is a subgroup of (Z/pZ)*; existence of multiplicative inverses mod p
ideas.where_published: E262; Euler himself says 'quae alibi fusius pertractavi' (§27)

ideas.what: The notation '..P' for an unspecified integer multiple of P.
ideas.usually_credited_to: Gauss 1801 for ≡; Euler's ad hoc notations are known

deep.surprise_reason: The page restates Euler's own well-documented group-theoretic proof of Fermat's little theorem and the subgroup properties of power residues. Euler himself flags these as already treated elsewhere (E262). Nothing on the page is new or uncredited.
transcription_corrections: Previous page: 'residuorum diuisorum' should read 'residuorum diuersorum' (distinct residues).
This page's transcription is essentially accurate. 'reliquat' in the image is 'relinquat'; the transcription has it correctly.
